Dissension
dĭs-sĕn'shun
n. (violent disagreement; a standing apart into parties; rendering Greek stasis)
Latin dissensio, from dis-, apart, and sentire, to feel or think — to think apart. The Greek stasis is stronger still: a standing, a faction, and in Roman ears a riot.

Biblical Definition

Luke uses the word three times, and every use is instructive. At Antioch, false teachers came down from Judaea binding circumcision on the Gentiles, and “Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them” (Act 15:2). That dissension was not sin; it was the gospel refusing to be added to, and it drove the church to the Jerusalem council where the truth was settled in writing. In the Sanhedrin, Paul's confession of the resurrection produced a different sort: “there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided” (Act 23:7), and it grew so violent that the chief captain feared Paul would be pulled in pieces (Act 23:10). Scripture therefore does not treat all division as evil. The word stasis can name a riot of the flesh or a stand for the faith. What decides is the thing stood for. Paul who stood against Peter to the face at Antioch is the same Paul who begs the Corinthians that there be no divisions among them. The rule is not peace at any price and not contention for its own sake, but truth held in love, and no small dissension when the gospel itself is at stake.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dissension as disagreement in opinion, usually a disagreement which produces warm debates or angry words; contention in words; strife; discord; quarrel; breach of friendship and union.

expand to see more

DISSENSION, n. Disagreement in opinion, usually a disagreement which is violent, producing warm debates or angry words; contention in words; strife; discord; quarrel; breach of friendship and union.

2. Political or ecclesiastical faction; a standing apart into parties.

Debates, dissension, uproars are thy joy.

Key Scripture

Act 15:2 — "When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question."

Act 23:7 — "And when he had so said, there arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees: and the multitude was divided."

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

Modern Corruption

Dissension is now treated as the worst sin a church can commit, so that the man who contends for the faith is the offender and the man who corrupts it is the peacemaker.

expand to see more

The modern instinct reads Acts 15:2 backwards. It sees Paul and Barnabas making no small dissension and concludes that Paul and Barnabas were the problem — that a humbler man would have absorbed the addition of circumcision for the sake of unity and spared the church a fight. Scripture judges otherwise: the Holy Ghost preserved that dissension in the record as the thing that produced the Jerusalem decree, and Galatians tells us plainly that giving place by subjection, no, not for an hour, was the only way the truth of the gospel might continue. The corruption is a counterfeit peace that treats every doctrinal contention as a failure of charity and every doctrinal surrender as maturity. It has a genuine mirror-image sin, and the dictionary names that too: the man who loves the fight, who finds a Sanhedrin in every congregation and calls his temper conviction. The test Scripture gives is the object. A dissension about the gospel is faithfulness; a dissension about preference, party, or personal standing is the flesh, and Paul calls it by that name in the list of Galatians 5:20.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stasis (G4714), a standing, faction, insurrection, dissension; zetesis (G2214), questioning, debate; schisma (G4978), a rent or split, the word behind “divisions” in 1 Corinthians 1:10.

expand to see more

Greek stasis (G4714) — a standing, a faction, an insurrection; the same noun describes Barabbas' sedition and the Sanhedrin's uproar; Acts 15:2, 23:7, 23:10.

Greek zetesis (G2214) — questioning, debate, controversy; the companion word in Acts 15:2, translated “disputation”.

Greek schisma (G4978) — a tear, a rent, as in an unshrunk cloth on an old garment; the word Paul forbids in the church; 1 Corinthians 1:10, 11:18.

Usage

"“No small dissension and disputation” — the contention that produced the Jerusalem council and guarded the gospel of grace."

"“There arose a dissension between the Pharisees and the Sadducees” — a council of the flesh dividing over a doctrine neither party held for God's sake."

"“That there be no divisions among you” — the apostolic charge that binds every congregation not contending for the faith itself."
